cards.title: What is a **metric prefix**, and what do **kilo-**, **centi-** and **milli-** mean?
cards.body:
A metric prefix is a short word-start that scales a unit by a power of ten: kilo- means $1000$ times, centi- means $\frac{1}{100}$ of, and milli- means $\frac{1}{1000}$ of.

A **unit** is the agreed amount we count in when we measure, such as the meter for length or the gram for mass. Prefixes give bigger and smaller versions of the same unit without inventing new names: $1\ \mathrm{km} = 1000\ \mathrm{m}$, $1\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.01\ \mathrm{m}$ and $1\ \mathrm{mm} = 0.001\ \mathrm{m}$.

Example: A $5\ \mathrm{km}$ walk is $5 \times 1000 = 5000\ \mathrm{m}$, and a $250\ \mathrm{cm}$ shelf is $250 \times 0.01 = 2.5\ \mathrm{m}$.

Tip: Every prefix is a power of ten, so converting inside the metric system only moves the decimal point.
cards.searchQuery: metric prefixes kilo centi milli meaning

cards.title: Why can you multiply by a **conversion factor** such as $\dfrac{1000\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{km}}$ without changing a length, and how do you chain several of them?
cards.body:
The factor is a fraction equal to $1$ (its top and bottom are the same amount written in different units), so multiplying by it changes the units but not the quantity. Chain factors so each unwanted unit cancels, until only the wanted unit is left.

Key idea: Write the units into the calculation and cancel them like numbers. If the unit you want is what remains, you set up the factors the right way up.

Example: Convert $3$ hours to seconds.

$$3\ \mathrm{h} \times \frac{60\ \mathrm{min}}{1\ \mathrm{h}} \times \frac{60\ \mathrm{s}}{1\ \mathrm{min}} = 10{,}800\ \mathrm{s}$$

Watch out: If the units don't cancel the way you wanted, you flipped a factor. Fix the fraction, not the answer.
cards.searchQuery: conversion factor unit cancel chain conversion

cards.title: Convert $90\ \mathrm{km/h}$ to meters per second by chaining conversion factors. (Give the number of $\mathrm{m/s}$.)
cards.body:
25

$$90\ \frac{\mathrm{km}}{\mathrm{h}} \times \frac{1000\ \mathrm{m}}{1\ \mathrm{km}} \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{h}}{3600\ \mathrm{s}} = \frac{90{,}000}{3600}\ \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}} = 25\ \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$$

The kilometers cancel in the first step and the hours cancel in the second, leaving meters over seconds. There are $60 \times 60 = 3600$ seconds in an hour.

Tip: Dividing by $3.6$ turns $\mathrm{km/h}$ into $\mathrm{m/s}$, because $\frac{1000}{3600} = \frac{1}{3.6}$.
cards.searchQuery: convert km/h to m/s conversion factors

cards.title: Why is it false that $1\ \mathrm{m}^2 = 100\ \mathrm{cm}^2$?
cards.body:
$1\ \mathrm{m}^2 = 10{,}000\ \mathrm{cm}^2$, and likewise $1\ \mathrm{m}^3 = 1{,}000{,}000\ \mathrm{cm}^3$: the length factor $100$ must be squared for area and cubed for volume.

A **square unit** is a square whose sides are one unit long; we measure the flat space a shape covers by counting them. A **cubic unit** is a cube with edges one unit long, used to measure the space inside a solid.

Why: A square $1\ \mathrm{m}$ on a side is also $100\ \mathrm{cm}$ on a side, so it holds $100 \times 100 = 10{,}000$ small squares. A cube $1\ \mathrm{m}$ on an edge holds $100 \times 100 \times 100 = 1{,}000{,}000$ small cubes. In symbols, $(100\ \mathrm{cm})^2 = 100^2\ \mathrm{cm}^2$.

Watch out: The $100$ converts lengths only. Whenever the unit is squared or cubed, the conversion factor is squared or cubed too.
cards.searchQuery: square meters to square centimeters 10000 conversion

cards.title: A tank holds $2\ \mathrm{m}^3$ of water. Given that $1$ liter $= 1000\ \mathrm{cm}^3$, how many liters is that? (Give the number.)
cards.body:
2000

First change cubic meters to cubic centimeters: $2\ \mathrm{m}^3 = 2 \times 1{,}000{,}000 = 2{,}000{,}000\ \mathrm{cm}^3$.

Then divide by the $1000\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ in each liter: $\dfrac{2{,}000{,}000}{1000} = 2000$ liters.

Key idea: $1\ \mathrm{m}^3$ is $1000$ liters, which is why a cubic meter of water is such a handy size to remember.

Watch out: Using $100$ instead of $1{,}000{,}000$ for the cubic conversion would give $0.2$ liters, a tiny tank for a whole cubic meter.
cards.searchQuery: cubic meters to liters conversion 1000 liters

cards.title: What is the **perimeter** of a flat shape, and what is its **area**?
cards.body:
Perimeter is the distance around the outside edge, measured in length units; area is how much flat space the shape covers, measured in square units.

Example: A rectangle $3\ \mathrm{cm}$ by $5\ \mathrm{cm}$ has perimeter $3 + 5 + 3 + 5 = 16\ \mathrm{cm}$. Its area is $3 \times 5 = 15\ \mathrm{cm}^2$, because it holds $3$ rows of $5$ unit squares.

Key idea: The area of a rectangle is length times width.

Tip: Fencing a garden needs the perimeter; covering it with turf needs the area.

Watch out: The units differ: $\mathrm{cm}$ for perimeter, $\mathrm{cm}^2$ for area. Two shapes can have the same perimeter and very different areas.
cards.searchQuery: perimeter versus area definition rectangle

cards.title: What is the area of a triangle with base $b$ and height $h$?
cards.body:
$A = \tfrac{1}{2}\,b\,h$

The height is the straight-line distance from the base to the opposite corner, measured at a right angle to the base, not along a slanted side.

Why: Two copies of the same triangle fit together into a parallelogram (a slanted rectangle) with base $b$ and height $h$. That parallelogram has area $bh$, so each triangle is half of it.

Example: A triangle with base $10\ \mathrm{cm}$ and height $6\ \mathrm{cm}$ has area $\frac{1}{2}(10)(6) = 30\ \mathrm{cm}^2$.

Tip: A trapezoid (a four-sided shape with one pair of parallel sides, meaning sides that run side by side and never meet) with parallel sides $a$ and $b$ and height $h$ has area $\frac{1}{2}(a + b)\,h$: the average of the parallel sides times the height.

Watch out: Don't use a slanted side as the height unless it happens to be at a right angle to the base.
cards.searchQuery: area of a triangle formula one half base height

cards.title: What are the **circumference** and the area of a circle with radius $r$?
cards.body:
$C = 2\pi r$ and $A = \pi r^2$

The **circumference** is the perimeter of a circle. The radius is the distance from the center to the edge. **Pi** ($\pi \approx 3.14159$) is the number you get by dividing any circle's circumference by its diameter; it is the same for every circle, and it is irrational.

Example: For $r = 5$, $C = 2\pi(5) = 10\pi \approx 31.4$ and $A = \pi(5)^2 = 25\pi \approx 78.5$.

Watch out: If you are given the diameter, halve it to get $r$ first. Squaring the diameter by mistake makes the area $4$ times too big.
cards.searchQuery: circle circumference 2 pi r area pi r squared

cards.title: A **prism** is a solid with two identical, parallel flat ends (its bases) joined by flat sides, so a box is a prism. A cylinder (a can) is the round version. Find the **volume** of a cylinder with radius $3\ \mathrm{cm}$ and height $10\ \mathrm{cm}$: give it in terms of $\pi$ and rounded to the nearest whole number.
cards.body:
$90\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^3 \approx 283\ \mathrm{cm}^3$

Volume is the amount of space inside a solid, measured in cubic units. For a prism or a cylinder, multiply the area of the base by the height: $V = (\text{base area}) \times h$. For a box this is $V = \ell \, w \, h$.

Solution: The base is a circle, so its area is $\pi r^2 = \pi(3)^2 = 9\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^2$. Then $V = 9\pi \times 10 = 90\pi \approx 282.7\ \mathrm{cm}^3$, which rounds to $283\ \mathrm{cm}^3$.

Key idea: Stack identical layers of the base shape, and the volume is one layer's area times the number of layers (the height).

Watch out: Use the radius, not the diameter, in $\pi r^2$.
cards.searchQuery: volume of a cylinder base area times height

cards.title: Why is it false that doubling every side of a rectangle doubles its area?
cards.body:
The area becomes $4$ times as large, because lengths multiply by $2$ and area multiplies by $2^2$.

Example: A $3 \times 5$ rectangle has area $15$. Doubling gives $6 \times 10$, with area $60 = 4 \times 15$. The perimeter only doubles, from $16$ to $32$.

For a box, doubling every edge multiplies the volume by $2^3 = 8$: a $2 \times 3 \times 4$ box has volume $24$, and a $4 \times 6 \times 8$ box has volume $192 = 8 \times 24$.

Key idea: Scaling every length by $k$ scales perimeter by $k$, area by $k^2$ and volume by $k^3$. It is the same reason $1\ \mathrm{m}^2 = 10{,}000\ \mathrm{cm}^2$.
cards.searchQuery: double side length area quadruples volume eight times

cards.title: What is a **degree**, and how many degrees is a **right angle**?
cards.body:
A degree is $\frac{1}{360}$ of a full turn, and a right angle (a square corner, a quarter turn) measures $90^\circ$.

An angle measures how much turn there is between two lines or rays that meet at a point. A half turn, or straight line, is $180^\circ$ and a full turn is $360^\circ$.

Example: An angle smaller than $90^\circ$ is called acute, and one between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ is called obtuse. The corner of a sheet of paper is a right angle.

Why: The number $360$ is a convenient choice because it divides evenly by many numbers, so common fractions of a turn come out as whole degrees.
cards.searchQuery: degree angle measure right angle 90 degrees

cards.title: Two straight lines cross and form four angles. How are two neighboring angles related, and how are two opposite angles related?
cards.body:
Neighboring angles add to $180^\circ$ (they are **supplementary angles**), and opposite angles are equal (they are **vertical angles**).

Why: Call one angle $x$. Each neighbor sits with it on a straight line, so each neighbor is $180^\circ - x$. The angle opposite to $x$ is a neighbor of a neighbor, so it equals $180^\circ - (180^\circ - x) = x$.

Example: If one angle is $70^\circ$, its two neighbors are $110^\circ$ each and the angle opposite it is $70^\circ$. Check: $70 + 110 + 70 + 110 = 360$.

Mnemonic: Two angles adding to $90^\circ$ are complementary (C for Corner), and two adding to $180^\circ$ are supplementary (S for Straight).
cards.searchQuery: vertical angles equal supplementary angles 180 degrees

cards.title: What is the **interior angle sum** of a polygon with $n$ sides?
cards.body:
$(n - 2) \times 180^\circ$

A polygon is a closed flat shape with straight sides, and its interior angles are the angles inside it at the corners. For a triangle, $n = 3$ gives the familiar sum of $180^\circ$; for a four-sided shape it gives $360^\circ$.

Why: Take a polygon whose corners all point outward. From one corner, draw lines to every corner that isn't next to it. This cuts the polygon into $n - 2$ triangles, and the angles of every triangle add to $180^\circ$. (The formula also holds for any polygon whose sides don't cross, even with corners pointing inward.)

Example: A hexagon has $n = 6$, so its angles add to $4 \times 180^\circ = 720^\circ$. If all six angles are equal, each is $720^\circ \div 6 = 120^\circ$.

Watch out: The formula gives the sum of the angles, not each angle. Divide by $n$ only when all the angles are equal.
cards.searchQuery: polygon interior angle sum formula n minus 2 times 180

cards.title: Two parallel lines (lines in the same flat plane that never meet) are crossed by a **transversal** (a third line that cuts both). One angle is $(2x + 20)^\circ$. The alternate interior angle (between the parallel lines, on the opposite side of the transversal, at the other crossing) is $(3x - 10)^\circ$. Find $x$ and the angle.
cards.body:
$x = 30$, and each of the two angles is $80^\circ$.

Key move: When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, alternate interior angles are equal. Corresponding angles (in the same position at each crossing) are also equal, and two interior angles on the same side of the transversal add to $180^\circ$.

Solution: Set them equal: $2x + 20 = 3x - 10$. Subtracting $2x$ and adding $10$ gives $x = 30$.

Check: $2(30) + 20 = 80$ and $3(30) - 10 = 80$.
cards.searchQuery: alternate interior angles parallel lines transversal solve for x

cards.title: Why is it false that alternate interior angles are always equal when a transversal crosses two lines?
cards.body:
They are equal only when the two lines are parallel; if the lines are not parallel, the angles differ.

Example: If a transversal makes alternate interior angles of $80^\circ$ and $70^\circ$ with two lines, those lines are not parallel. They tilt toward each other and would meet if extended.

The fact also runs backwards: if the alternate interior angles are equal, the lines must be parallel. That is how you can prove two lines are parallel.

Watch out: Use the equal-angle rules only when the problem says the lines are parallel (or you have shown it). Don't assume parallel lines because a diagram looks that way.
cards.searchQuery: alternate interior angles equal only if lines parallel

cards.title: State the **Pythagorean theorem**.
cards.body:
In a right triangle with legs $a$ and $b$ and hypotenuse $c$, $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

A **right triangle** has one right angle ($90^\circ$). Its two **legs** are the sides that meet at the right angle, and the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite the right angle, which is always the longest side.

Why: The area of the square built on the hypotenuse equals the areas of the squares on the two legs added together.

Example: Legs $6$ and $8$ give $c^2 = 36 + 64 = 100$, so $c = 10$.

Tip: To find a missing leg, subtract: $a^2 = c^2 - b^2$.
cards.searchQuery: Pythagorean theorem right triangle a squared plus b squared

cards.title: A right triangle has a leg of $10$ and a hypotenuse of $26$. How long is the other leg? (Give the number.)
cards.body:
24

$10^2 + b^2 = 26^2$, so $b^2 = 676 - 100 = 576$ and $b = 24$.

A **Pythagorean triple** is three positive whole numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ with $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. The best known are $3\text{-}4\text{-}5$ and $5\text{-}12\text{-}13$, and also $8\text{-}15\text{-}17$ and $7\text{-}24\text{-}25$.

Multiplying every number in a triple by the same whole number gives another triple. Here $10\text{-}24\text{-}26$ is $2$ times $5\text{-}12\text{-}13$.

Tip: When a problem shows numbers like $5$ and $13$, or $6$ and $8$, check for a triple (possibly scaled) before doing any arithmetic.
cards.searchQuery: Pythagorean triples 3 4 5 5 12 13 scaled

cards.title: What are the side ratios of the two **special right triangles**, 45-45-90 and 30-60-90?
cards.body:
45-45-90: $x : x : x\sqrt{2}$ (leg, leg, hypotenuse). 30-60-90: $x : x\sqrt{3} : 2x$ (shortest leg, other leg, hypotenuse).

Why: In a 45-45-90 triangle the legs are equal, so $c^2 = x^2 + x^2 = 2x^2$ and $c = x\sqrt{2}$. A 30-60-90 triangle is half of an equilateral triangle with side $2x$, cut down the middle: the hypotenuse is $2x$, the short leg is $x$, and the other leg is $\sqrt{(2x)^2 - x^2} = x\sqrt{3}$.

Example: A 45-45-90 triangle with legs $7$ has hypotenuse $7\sqrt{2} \approx 9.9$. A 30-60-90 triangle with hypotenuse $10$ has shortest leg $5$ and other leg $5\sqrt{3}$.

Watch out: The shortest leg is opposite the $30^\circ$ angle, and the hypotenuse is the side with the factor $2$, never the one with $\sqrt{3}$.
cards.searchQuery: 45-45-90 30-60-90 special right triangle side ratios

cards.title: The **converse** of the Pythagorean theorem says: if the sides of a triangle satisfy $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, then it is a right triangle with hypotenuse $c$. Use it to decide whether triangles with sides $9, 40, 41$ and $6, 8, 11$ are right triangles.
cards.body:
The $9, 40, 41$ triangle is a right triangle; the $6, 8, 11$ triangle is not.

Key move: Put the longest side in the role of $c$ and compare $a^2 + b^2$ with $c^2$.

Solution: For $9, 40, 41$: $81 + 1600 = 1681 = 41^2$, so it is right. For $6, 8, 11$: $36 + 64 = 100$, but $11^2 = 121$, so it is not.

Tip: If $c^2$ is bigger than $a^2 + b^2$ (as here), the angle opposite $c$ is more than $90^\circ$; if it is smaller (with $c$ the longest side), all the angles are less than $90^\circ$.

Watch out: Never test with a shorter side as $c$. The test needs the longest side on the right-hand side.
cards.searchQuery: converse Pythagorean theorem test right triangle sides

cards.title: Why is it false that the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs $3$ and $4$ is $3 + 4 = 7$?
cards.body:
The theorem adds the squares of the legs, not the legs: $c = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$.

Why: In general $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ is smaller than $a + b$ for positive $a$ and $b$, because $(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$ has the extra piece $2ab$. Geometrically, going straight across the hypotenuse is shorter than walking along both legs.

Watch out: Two slips are common. One is adding the lengths. The other is stopping at $a^2 + b^2 = 25$ and forgetting the final square root.

Example: Legs $3$ and $4$ give a hypotenuse of $5$, and $5 < 7$.
cards.searchQuery: Pythagorean theorem common mistake add legs square root

cards.title: Define the **median**, the **mode** and the **range** of a data set.
cards.body:
Median: the middle value once the data are sorted (the mean of the two middle values when there is an even number of them). Mode: the value that appears most often. Range: the largest value minus the smallest.

Example: For $2, 5, 3, 5, 9$, sorted as $2, 3, 5, 5, 9$, the median is $5$, the mode is $5$ and the range is $9 - 2 = 7$. For the even-sized set $2, 3, 5, 9$ the median is $\frac{3 + 5}{2} = 4$.

Median, mode and the mean (next card) are all called averages: each is one number meant to represent a typical value.

Watch out: Sort before finding the median. A data set can have no mode (all values appear once) or several. The range measures spread, not a typical value.
cards.searchQuery: median mode range definition data set

cards.title: How do you compute the **mean** of $n$ numbers, and how can you recover their total from the mean?
cards.body:
$\text{mean} = \dfrac{\text{sum of the values}}{n}$, so the total is $\text{mean} \times n$.

Why: The mean is the value each number would have if the total were shared out equally.

Example: Scores $80, 90, 70, 100$ add to $340$, so the mean is $\frac{340}{4} = 85$. If $5$ numbers have mean $12$, their sum is $5 \times 12 = 60$.

Tip: To average $85$ over $5$ tests, you need a total of $5 \times 85 = 425$. Subtract what you already have to see what the remaining tests must add up to.
cards.searchQuery: mean average formula sum divided by count

cards.title: What is an **outlier**, and why does it move the mean much more than the median?
cards.body:
An outlier is a value far away from the rest of the data; it changes the sum, which the mean counts in full, while the median depends only on the middle position.

Example: The data $3, 4, 5, 6, 7$ have mean $5$ and median $5$. Replace $7$ with $100$: the mean becomes $\frac{118}{5} = 23.6$, but the median is still $5$.

Tip: Choosing a suitable average: for data with a few huge values, like house prices or incomes, the median describes a typical value better. For evenly spread data the mean works well. For categories, such as the most common shirt size, use the mode.
cards.searchQuery: outlier effect on mean versus median

cards.title: Find the mean, median, mode and range of $12, 7, 9, 7, 15, 10$.
cards.body:
Mean $10$, median $9.5$, mode $7$, range $8$.

Sort first: $7, 7, 9, 10, 12, 15$.

- Mean: the sum is $60$ and there are $6$ values, so $\frac{60}{6} = 10$.
- Median: with $6$ values, average the middle two: $\frac{9 + 10}{2} = 9.5$.
- Mode: $7$ appears twice and every other value once.
- Range: $15 - 7 = 8$.

Watch out: With an even number of values, the median usually isn't one of the data values.
cards.searchQuery: find mean median mode range worked example

cards.title: Class A has $2$ students with a mean score of $90$; class B has $8$ students with a mean of $60$. Why is the combined mean not $\frac{90 + 60}{2} = 75$?
cards.body:
The classes differ in size, so the larger class counts for more; the combined mean is $\frac{2 \cdot 90 + 8 \cdot 60}{10} = 66$.

Why: A mean is a total divided by a count. Recover each class's total with $\text{mean} \times \text{count}$: $180$ for A and $480$ for B. The combined total is $660$ over $10$ students.

Watch out: Averaging the averages works only when the groups have the same size.

Key idea: Combine totals and counts, not means.
cards.searchQuery: average of averages different group sizes combined mean
